title: Getting liquidity where it is needed − speech by Nathanaël Benjamin
summary: Bank of England Executive Director Nathanaël Benjamin delivered a speech at OMFIF on the evolving liquidity landscape, highlighting how non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) now account for roughly half of financial system assets globally and in the UK, while market-based finance accounts for essentially all UK corporate credit growth since the GFC. The speech addresses structural shifts in liquidity flows, derivatives market liquidity risks from margin calls in stress, repo market haircut dynamics, and the Bank's transition from an abundant-reserves framework to a repo-led operating framework.
key_points: NBFIs now account for approximately half of total financial system assets, both globally and in the UK
UK corporate credit growth since the Global Financial Crisis has been entirely in market-based finance, which now represents 50% of the stock of corporate lending
Bank of England's reserves have declined from a peak of roughly £980bn to approximately £680bn as QT and TFSME repayments progress
TFSME outstanding has declined from £193bn to £83bn as banks repay or allow schemes to mature
Aggregate LCRs remain robust at 153% for large banks and 285% for smaller banks despite shrinking reserve supply
The Bank is transitioning to a repo-led operating framework where balance sheet size reflects system liquidity needs rather than fixed quantitative targets
Derivatives market reforms post-GFC reduced counterparty risk but increased liquidity risks from margin calls in stress scenarios, with more of this risk now sitting with NBFIs
why_it_matters: This speech articulates the BoE's analytical framework for understanding how liquidity flows through an evolving financial system where non-bank institutions play a significantly larger role. It signals that traditional focus on bank liquidity is insufficient—policymakers now explicitly monitor NBFI liquidity resilience, repo market functioning, and margin call dynamics as critical infrastructure. The transition away from abundant reserves means banks and non-banks must adapt liquidity management practices, with implications for gilt demand, repo market functioning, and short-term funding costs.
market_structure_context: The speech provides the BoE's analytical perspective on structural changes to UK liquidity infrastructure: (1) NBFIs now represent ~50% of financial system assets globally and in the UK, changing who holds and needs liquidity; (2) market-based finance has grown from minimal levels to 50% of UK corporate lending stock; (3) derivatives market reforms reduced counterparty risk but increased liquidity risks from margin calls in stress scenarios; (4) repo market mechanics including haircut risk in stress environments; (5) transition from reserves-abundant framework to repo-led operations; (6) larger banks replacing central bank reserves with gilts in HQLA portfolios; (7) BoE's Short-Term Repo (STR) and Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) facilities as tools to smooth money market frictions.
